http://127.0.0.1:1024/en/blog/code-monke.body:
For a long time, a developer’s daily life often came down to one thing: turning an idea into lines of code by hand, loop by loop, semicolon by semicolon.
Today, any LLM can generate a function or a UI in three seconds. Typing code by the mile no longer has any value. The job isn’t dead, but its focus is shifting radically.
Less syntax, more judgment🔗
Generating code has become free. Maintaining and understanding it remains costly. Day to day, our time no longer goes into hunting for syntax or boilerplate code, but into three essential topics:
Expressing the need clearly: If the instruction is vague, the AI produces a bad solution in a flash. Precision in modeling and business rules matters more than ever.
Reviewing with a critical eye: Generated code often looks clean at first glance. That’s misleading: edge cases, security holes, or logical nonsense hide easily inside it. Our main role has become that of a ruthless reviewer.
Hardening the tests: To trust code you didn’t type yourself, you need solid tests (unit, integration, strict typing). The test harness becomes our safety net.
The big picture rather than the isolated brick🔗
AI is good at coding one specific function, but it has a short memory and doesn’t see the big picture. Architecture choices, module breakdown, infra cost management, and database consistency remain purely human decisions.
If you let agents stack code without any control, you quickly end up with an unmanageable codebase that nobody masters: tech debt on autopilot.
What about beginners?🔗
That’s probably the real pain point. You used to become senior by breaking things and spending nights hunting for a bug in your own code.
For a junior today, the trap is using AI as a crutch without ever understanding what runs under the hood. The key to learning is shifting: it’s less about writing from a blank page than about learning to read, debug, and challenge what gets generated.
In short🔗
The job doesn’t disappear, it sheds its most mechanical part. Less time wasted on basic plumbing, more energy invested in design, robustness, and value for the user.
http://127.0.0.1:1024/en/blog/code-monke.title: From « Code Monkey » to Systemic Orchestrator: how the developer job is changing

http://127.0.0.1:1024/en/blog/deepseek-f.body:
Let me be blunt: DeepSeek’s latest model, Flash 4.1, kind of blew my mind.
We’re used to DeepSeek shipping solid models at ridiculous prices. But this time, they went one step further, and not a small one.
Open source, for real🔗
The first thing is that Flash 4.1 is open source. Not “half open weights”, not “open but with a license that forbids you from using it for work”. No: the weights are there, you can download them, host them yourself, fine-tune them, run them on your own infra.
That’s a huge difference. When you depend on a closed API, you depend on someone else: their prices, their terms, their outages, their dumb model changes that break your production overnight. Here, you stay in control.
And the price…🔗
That’s the second point, and probably the most annoying one for the competition.
Flash 4.1 costs a fraction of what the American models charge, for a level of quality that, honestly, has little left to envy them for on most everyday tasks. Generating code, writing, summarizing, extracting data, holding a conversation: for 90% of real use cases, the difference has become hard to justify.
When an open, nearly free model does the same job as a closed model billed ten times more, at some point you need a real reason to pay. “It’s a US model” is no longer one.
Real competition for the American models🔗
That’s where it gets interesting. The big American players (OpenAI, Anthropic, Google) built their business on two pillars: performance, and being the only ones able to deliver it.
The first pillar still holds, but less and less. The second one is collapsing.
Because DeepSeek’s strategy is brutal: they publish openly, they slash prices, and they force everyone to go back to the drawing board. Other labs now have to either lower their rates or justify added value that no longer exists for most customers. That’s enormous pressure, and it comes from a player that, only a few years ago, wasn’t even in the race.
What it changes for us🔗
Concretely, for someone like me who tinkers with projects, writes scripts, and uses AI to rough out work: it means we can stop counting every token as if it were gold.
We can test, make mistakes, iterate, and re-run generations without it hurting our wallet. We can also host the model ourselves if we have sensitive data and don’t want to send it off to a third-party provider. In short, we get control back.
Fair warning, though🔗
I’m not going to fall into fanboyism either. An open source model means you handle the infra, the updates, the security. It’s not magic. And on the most demanding tasks, the American frontier models still keep a lead.
But for everything else, the question is no longer “is open source good enough?”. The question has become “why would I pay full price for this?”.
In short🔗
Flash 4.1 isn’t just a good model. It’s a signal: quality is becoming commoditized, prices are collapsing, and the closed American models are going to have to learn to live with competition they no longer control.
And honestly, that’s good news for everyone. Except for their margins.
http://127.0.0.1:1024/en/blog/deepseek-f.title: DeepSeek Flash 4.1: the open source model putting pressure on the American players

http://127.0.0.1:1024/en/blog/herdr-term.body:
With the rise of AI coding agents (Claude Code, GitHub Copilot CLI, Cursor Agent…), the way we work in the terminal is changing fast. Running several agents in parallel inside a classic multiplexer (like tmux or zellij) quickly becomes messy when you need to track who’s doing what. That’s where Herdr comes in.
What is Herdr?🔗
Herdr is a persistent terminal multiplexer built specifically for the age of AI agents. It runs as a background server and adds an agent-aware management layer on top of your usual PTYs.
What Herdr lets you do🔗
🚦 Real-time status tracking: Herdr automatically detects each agent’s state and displays it clearly (running, waiting for input, blocked, or done). No more endless scrolling to figure out whether an agent needs you!
🔄 Absolute persistence: Your tasks keep running even if you close your terminal window or disconnect an SSH session.
🔌 API & automation: Through its CLI and socket API, agents can themselves interact with the multiplexer (open new tabs, launch sub-tasks).
🖥️ Native terminal: It integrates seamlessly with your favorite terminal emulator using standard PTYs.
In short🔗
If you use AI agents in the CLI every day for your projects and want to maximize your productivity without losing track, Herdr is a tool you should try right away.
http://127.0.0.1:1024/en/blog/herdr-term.title: Herdr: the terminal multiplexer built for AI agents 🤖
